drills.q: An Athena table costs $4,500/month. What are the first three things you check, in order?
drills.a: 1) File format -- is it Parquet/ORC (columnar) or raw CSV/JSON (row-oriented, reads everything). 2) Compression -- is Snappy or gzip applied. 3) Partitioning -- does the table have a partition column (usually date) that queries actually filter on. These three together commonly produce 90%+ reduction in bytes scanned, which is the entire Athena bill.

drills.q: What's the difference between what Firehose and Kinesis Data Streams let you do with the same event stream?
drills.a: Kinesis Data Streams is a durable, replayable stream that up to 8 independent consumers can read from within the retention window (24h default, up to 365 days). Firehose is a one-way managed delivery pipe to a single destination (S3, Redshift, OpenSearch) with automatic format conversion and batching, but it cannot be read back or replayed by a second consumer -- if you need multiple consumers or replay, Firehose alone can't do it.

drills.q: A Glue ETL job that used to run in 20 minutes for $8.80 now takes 3 hours and costs $75+ with no data volume increase. Diagnose.
drills.a: Most likely cause is partition/data skew -- one Spark executor doing disproportionately more work than the rest while others sit idle, often from a join key or groupby key with a heavily skewed value distribution, or a shuffle-heavy join lacking a broadcast hint for a small table. Check the Spark UI for stage-level task duration variance; the fix is repartitioning on a better key or adding a broadcast join hint. If this keeps recurring, it's also a signal the job may be better suited to EMR where you have more granular Spark tuning control.

drills.q: Why does 'cluster-billed vs query-billed' matter more than raw feature comparison when choosing between Redshift and Athena for a new analytics workload?
drills.a: Because it determines what your cost curve looks like against usage pattern, not just what queries you can run. A cluster-billed system (Redshift, outside Serverless) charges for provisioned time regardless of query volume -- great for steady, high-concurrency BI workloads, terrible for spiky or rare ad hoc queries where you'd pay for idle capacity. A query-billed system (Athena) charges only for bytes scanned -- zero cost when idle, but no low-latency persistent compute for high-concurrency dashboard use. Picking based on feature checklist (both can run SQL joins) misses that the economics diverge completely depending on query frequency and concurrency shape.

drills.q: Your team has an existing Kafka Streams application with custom serializers and Kafka Connect sinks. Someone proposes migrating to Kinesis Data Streams for 'AWS-native simplicity.' What's your response?
drills.a: Push back unless there's a specific unmet need Kinesis solves that MSK doesn't -- migration cost of rewriting Kafka Streams topology, custom serializers, and Kafka Connect sinks to Kinesis-native equivalents (which don't have a 1:1 mapping for most of that tooling) consistently exceeds the operational benefit of avoiding MSK's broker management, especially since AWS manages the MSK broker infrastructure already. Recommend MSK unless the actual driver is something Kinesis does that Kafka fundamentally can't (e.g. specific AWS-native IAM integration requirements).

drills.q: Design a pipeline for: a table with 3 years of daily-partitioned clickstream data, where the Glue crawler now takes 25 minutes to run and the partition count in the catalog is over 1 million.
drills.a: Migrate the table to partition projection instead of registered/crawled partitions. Since the partitions are predictable (year/month/day), configure projection.dt.type=date with a range and format, and set storage.location.template to compute the S3 path algorithmically. This removes the need to run the crawler on this table at all (partitions are computed at query time, not stored as catalog metadata), which both eliminates the 25-minute crawler cost and removes the per-query metadata-lookup overhead Athena was paying against a million-partition catalog entry.

drills.q: A Redshift cluster is 'healthy' by CPU/memory metrics but query queuing is increasing under normal load. What do you check first and why?
drills.a: Distribution key choice on the tables involved in the slow queries' joins. A DISTKEY mismatch forces a cross-node shuffle on every join referencing that table, which shows up as query latency and queuing rather than as CPU/memory pressure on any single node -- the cluster looks healthy in aggregate because the cost is network/shuffle time, not compute saturation. Check SVV_TABLE_INFO or Redshift Advisor for dist/sort key recommendations before considering a cluster resize, since resizing compute doesn't fix a shuffle-bound query pattern.

drills.q: When would you deliberately choose OpenSearch over a purpose-built vector database for a RAG system, given that a dedicated vector DB is usually less operational surface?
drills.a: When the production retrieval pattern is genuinely hybrid -- combining BM25 lexical scoring with vector similarity in a single query, which is the pattern that beats pure vector search on retrieval quality in most production RAG systems -- or when the team is already operating OpenSearch for logs/full-text search and vector search is incremental cost on infrastructure that already exists, rather than a new operational commitment.

drills.q: Explain why Redshift Spectrum querying an S3 table doesn't reduce your RA3 managed storage bill even if you stop loading new data into the cluster.
drills.a: Because Spectrum queries data in place in S3 without ever loading it into the cluster's managed storage -- it's a separate query path, not an ingestion mechanism. If your goal is to reduce managed storage costs by moving cold data to S3, you need to actually UNLOAD or delete the data from Redshift's managed storage and re-point queries at the S3 copy via Spectrum; simply adding Spectrum access to an S3 table alongside existing loaded data does nothing to the existing managed storage footprint.

drills.q: A monthly reporting workload causes huge concurrent query bursts against an otherwise near-idle warehouse. Compare provisioned Redshift, Redshift Serverless, and Athena for this shape.
drills.a: Provisioned Redshift means paying 24/7 for burst-capacity headroom that sits idle most of the month -- poor fit. Redshift Serverless bills per RPU-second consumed, giving the low-latency BI-dashboard experience only when actually queried -- strong fit as long as the burst doesn't exceed the workgroup's max RPU ceiling (if it does, provisioned Redshift with concurrency scaling is the fallback). Athena would be cost-efficient for the idle periods but loses the sub-second, connection-pooled, BI-tool-friendly query experience that Redshift's engine is built for, so it's a weaker fit if dashboard responsiveness during the burst matters.
